title: Analyzing and Rewarding Credit Card Spending Habits in India: a Machine Learning Approach
authors: Agrawal, R.; Khanna, A.; Hamdare, S.
venue: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
tldr: ML techniques including K-Means clustering and regression models analyze Indian credit card spending patterns to optimize personalized reward point allocation, achieving an R2 value of 0.99.
problem_and_motivation: Traditional credit card reward programs use one-size-fits-all structures that fail to differentiate between high-value and nominal spenders, resulting in missed opportunities for customer engagement and retention. Existing models lack adaptability to evolving user preferences and overlook discretionary spending categories such as luxury and travel. There is a gap in developing tailored systems that use machine learning to optimize sales and reward structures for credit card companies.
approach: Analyzed the original Kaggle credit card spending dataset and identified limitations including missing user IDs, outdated 2014-2015 dates, and lack of contextual features.
Generated a synthetic dataset using Python's Faker library with 16 features including user ID, card type, expense type, income category, and attrition risk.
Applied K-Means clustering with K=4 to segment users by card type using monthly spend, transactions per month, and credit utilization as features.
Compared K-Means against DBSCAN, Hierarchical, and GMM clustering using Silhouette Scores and Davies-Bouldin Index.
Designed a multi-factor reward points formula incorporating card type multiplier, promotion status, expense type, income category, number of cards, and attrition risk.
Applied Linear Regression, Random Forest, and XGBoost models to predict reward points on the synthetic dataset.
Validated the proposed reward formula by comparing ML model predictions against manually calculated reward points.
Conducted a case study comparing original versus synthetic reward calculations for a Signature cardholder spending 50,000 monthly.
findings: num: K-Means achieved a Silhouette Score of 0.42, outperforming DBSCAN, Hierarchical, and GMM clustering techniques.
num: Random Forest and XGBoost both achieved an R2 value of 0.99 for reward point prediction, with Random Forest having the lowest RMSE and MAE.
num: Synthetic dataset reward points range from 0 to 3500, compared to a maximum of 1000 in the original dataset.
num: Mean reward points increased to approximately 1000 with the synthetic dataset's additional features.
num: A Signature cardholder spending 50,000 monthly received 650 points with the synthetic formula versus 400 with the original formula.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a multi-factor reward points formula that incorporates card type, expense category, income level, promotion status, and attrition risk for personalized reward allocation. It demonstrates that K-Means clustering based on card type effectively segments credit card users into distinct spending behavioral profiles. The study validates the approach using Random Forest, XGBoost, and Linear Regression, achieving an R2 of 0.99 for reward point prediction. It also provides a methodology for generating synthetic financial datasets to overcome limitations of publicly available credit card transaction data.
directly_justifies: K-Means clustering with K=4 effectively segments users by card type based on spending behavior.
Synthetic datasets with additional features produce more systematic and justified reward distributions than original datasets.
Random Forest achieves the lowest RMSE and MAE among tested models for reward point prediction.
Multi-factor reward formulas incorporating expense type, income, and attrition risk outperform card-type-only calculations.
Festive season spending peaks (Diwali, Christmas, Holi) justify temporal reward adjustments.
limits: Results are based on synthetic data rather than real credit card transaction records.
Reward multipliers are subjective approximations since banks do not disclose actual values.
Only four clustering algorithms were compared, limiting generalizability of segmentation findings.
The study focuses on the Indian market, which may not generalize to other demographic contexts.
The R2 of 0.99 on synthetic data may overstate model performance relative to real-world deployment.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. Domain 3 (Expense Categorization) was flagged as high relevance due to the paper's core focus on expense category frameworks for reward allocation (3.A) and category design considerations (3.B). Domain 5 (Financial Behavioral Profiles) was flagged as high for behavioral profiling (5.A) and classification approaches (5.C) given the K-Means user segmentation. Domain 6 (Predictive Modeling) was flagged as high for predictive modeling (6.A) and medium for sequential forecasting (6.B) based on the ML models and monthly trend analysis. Domain 11 (Engagement) was medium for engagement dynamics (11.A) and retention mechanisms (11.B) due to the reward-driven retention design. Domain 12 (Evaluation) was high for algorithmic evaluation (12.B) with comprehensive metric reporting. Domain 14 (Synthetic Data) was high for synthetic data generation (14.A). Domains 1 (Filipino Young Professionals), 2.D (Filipino Spending Cycles), 7 (Budgeting), 8 (Anomaly Detection), 9 (Mobile Design), 10 (Privacy), 13 (Savings/Debt), and 14.B-C (Model Serving, On-Device) were considered and rejected as the paper does not address these topics. Domain 2.B (Seasonal Spending) was considered but assigned low relevance as festive spending is mentioned but not the primary focus. Overall, the paper covers expense categorization, behavioral profiling, predictive modeling, engagement design, and synthetic data generation in the context of credit card reward optimization.
